strengths: Addresses a practically important problem of zero-shot generalization in generative retrieval with well-motivated solutions
Comprehensive and systematic empirical evaluation across 69 MAIR tasks and BEIR benchmarks with detailed ablations (Sections 6.3-6.6)
Valuable large-scale resource: ZeroGR-Train dataset (41M query-document pairs, 6 domains) is the largest open-source IR corpus to date

Well-designed three-component framework with coherent motivation: unified docid representation handles heterogeneity, instruction conditioning addresses query distribution gap, reverse annealing balances precision-recall
Achieves competitive performance with smaller models (3B parameters) compared to 7B-parameter baselines, demonstrating parameter efficiency
Outperforms OpenAI Embed-v3-Small on zero-shot MAIR benchmark (41.1 vs 40.6), demonstrating practical effectiveness
Clear presentation with reproducible methodology; authors commit to releasing code and data
weaknesses: Limited core technical novelty: components are primarily engineering applications (LLM-based summaries for docids, instruction-conditioned query generation similar to DSI-QG, sigmoid-based temperature scheduling) rather than fundamental algorithmic innovations
Weaker generalization on BEIR unseen tasks: nDCG@10 (48.1) significantly underperforms instruction-tuned dense retrievers (E5-mistral-7B: 55.7), undermining claims of strong zero-shot generalization

Training data leakage concern: ZeroGR-Train includes data from MAIR training splits; unseen subset may not represent truly novel task distributions, limiting evidence for genuine out-of-distribution generalization

Insufficient justification of key design choices: reverse annealing (Eq. 6) lacks theoretical motivation, Figure 6 shows only modest improvements over simpler methods, no analysis of docid collision handling
Incomplete baseline comparisons: other GR methods (GENRE, GENRET, GLEN) have missing results across tables, limiting assessment of relative position in GR landscape

Lacking deeper analysis: minimal error analysis/failure cases, no qualitative evaluation of generated queries, no sensitivity analysis to instruction format/quality despite dependency on this component
Missing experimental rigor: no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals, fixed hyperparameters across tasks, minimal details on GPT-4o synthetic data curation process
Scalability and practical concerns: docid generation depends on GPT-4o (cost/availability), no inference efficiency analysis vs. dense retrievers, unclear applicability to massive real-world corpora
Docid conflict rates shown to decrease with training diversity (Figure 4) but impact on retrieval performance not analyzed; collision handling mechanism during inference not clearly specified
Insufficient ablation on key factors: temperature scheduling form not compared against simpler alternatives, saturation point for queries per document (Figure 5 middle) not thoroughly investigated

strengths: Addresses important problem of zero-shot generalization in generative retrieval with a well-motivated three-component framework
Introduces OpenInstIR, a valuable large-scale open-source instruction-tuning dataset (41M pairs, 69 tasks, 6 domains)—largest such resource to date
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with systematic ablations examining task diversity, docid design, decoding strategies, and scaling effects
Well-chosen diverse baselines spanning sparse, single-task dense, multi-task dense, and instruction-tuned models
Achieves competitive performance on MAIR benchmarks (41.1 Acc@1, on par with OpenAI-Embed-v3)
Clear and well-structured presentation with detailed implementation details and honest acknowledgment of limitations
weaknesses: Technical novelty is incremental: docid generation via LLM summarization, instruction-tuned pseudo-query generation, and temperature-based decoding are largely combinations of existing techniques with limited fundamental innovation

Significant performance gaps to state-of-the-art methods: 6-7 point gap on BEIR (48.1 vs 54-55 nDCG@10) and 6 point gap on MAIR compared to instruction-tuned baselines like E5-Mistral-7B and GritLM-7B

Critical scalability limitations unaddressed: evaluation limited to 'moderately sized corpora,' explicitly acknowledges no evaluation on >1M document corpora, raising concerns for real-world deployment
Model size gap undermines competitiveness: largest tested model is 3B parameters while competitive baselines use 7B; only marginal comparison provided

Dataset construction and validation concerns: OpenInstIR built from existing dataset training splits, instruction annotation quality not validated, evaluation set contains 17 document/query types unseen during training
Reverse annealing decoding shows marginal improvements in Figure 5 (essentially tied with greedy/beam on primary metrics), limiting contribution novelty
High performance variance across tasks (Table 8): some domains perform notably worse (Legal 40.0 Acc@1, Apple -8.22 degradation), suggesting poor generalization in certain settings
Missing reproducibility elements: code URL missing, hyperparameter specifications incomplete, and reverse annealing parameters (k, m) not fully specified for different configurations
Limited analysis of failure modes and qualitative examples; no inter-annotator agreement or human evaluation of instruction quality
No statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or ablations on docid generator training data quality

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing zero-shot generalization in generative retrieval, which is practically important and relatively unexplored

Thoughtfully designed three-component system with principled approach: unified docid generator handles heterogeneous documents elegantly, instruction-tuned query generator mitigates distribution gaps, and reverse annealing provides principled precision-recall tradeoff
Significant resource contribution: OpenInstIR is a large-scale (41M pairs, 69 tasks, 6 domains) open-source instruction dataset that will benefit the community

Comprehensive and systematic ablation studies rigorously examining task diversity (Figure 2), docid designs (Figure 3), decoding strategies (Figure 5), and model/query scaling—providing clear insights into design choices
Competitive results on MAIR benchmark (41.1 Acc@1) achieving parity with OpenAI-Embed-v3, demonstrating effective zero-shot generalization across diverse tasks
Strong reproducibility: detailed implementation details, hyperparameters, comprehensive appendices, and promised code release
Proper experimental methodology with multiple benchmarks, appropriate train/dev/test splits, and diverse baselines spanning sparse, dense, multi-task, and instruction-tuned methods
weaknesses: Substantial performance gap on BEIR benchmark (48.1 vs. 55.7 for E5-mistral-7B, +7.6 nDCG@10 difference), raising questions about practical competitiveness with dense retrieval on standard zero-shot benchmarks

Critical evaluation limitation: explicitly restricted to 'moderately sized corpora,' with no experiments on large-scale collections (>100K documents, certainly not millions); this limits generalizability and practical deployment feasibility claims

Heavy dependence on query generation quality (Figure 3, middle) with insufficient analysis of performance degradation on genuinely out-of-distribution queries or when query generator encounters unobserved query distributions

Limited technical novelty in individual components: unified docid generation via LLM summarization is straightforward; instruction-tuned query generation follows standard fine-tuning; reverse annealing is most novel but represents incremental improvement over beam search
High indexing cost (1.8h for 100K documents, Table 10) compared to dense retrieval (8 min), raising concerns about practical scalability and dynamic corpus scenarios despite amortization arguments

Loose 'zero-shot' terminology: training on 69 IR tasks makes this better characterized as 'few-task' or 'instruction-generalization' rather than truly zero-shot; strong assumption that task instructions are always available
Insufficient analysis of failure cases: no qualitative error analysis, limited discussion of domain-specific underperformance, and unexplained variance across tasks (e.g., Apple: 40→5.48 in Table 13)

Sparse details on OpenInstIR construction: vague instruction creation procedure ('following MAIR'), no human evaluation of instruction quality, potential consistency issues, and incomplete documentation of sampling/balancing strategies

Incomplete scaling analysis: model size scaling only extends to 3B (unclear if trends hold at 7B+), query diversity improvements plateau around 8-16 without quantifying diminishing returns, task diversity scaling lacks saturation analysis
No statistical significance testing reported (confidence intervals or hypothesis tests), and missing comparisons with some recent instruction-tuned dense retrievers under identical protocols
